messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Vignette:
At 55, Darnell had spent most of his adult life in work that required calm hands, exact thinking, and a tolerance for danger that other people could scarcely imagine. As a bomb disposal technician, he was used to reading a scene for risk before anyone else could, yet the event that altered him was not one he had been trained for. Years earlier, while working in an area struck by a natural disaster, he was caught in the chaos of an unpredictable collapse of the environment around him: the ground gave way, structures failed without warning, and the scene became a blur of noise, confusion, and sudden threat. What stayed with him was not a complete story but fragments — the sense of impact, the helpless urgency of not knowing what would fail next, and the raw bodily conviction that everything had become unsafe in an instant. Even now, when he tried to tell it, he found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully bring it into focus, as though his mind would not let him stay with the whole event for long. He could recall pieces — the sounds, the disarray, the feeling that he was moving through a disaster that could change shape at any second — but the rest felt missing, and that incompleteness frustrated him. When he did manage to think about it, he often felt a surge of intense rage, not only at what had happened but at the sheer injustice of how quickly ordinary reality had been ripped open.

In the months that followed, Darnell noticed that certain moments in daily life pulled him back toward that experience with unsettling force. Unpredictable situations were the hardest: a sudden interruption, an unexpected change in plans, or a noise he had not prepared for could jolt him as if danger had arrived in the room. Shouting had become especially hard to tolerate. If someone raised their voice on a street corner, in a store, or even in the parking lot outside his home, he found himself tensing before he had time to reason it through. Loud noises worked on him the same way. A bang from somewhere nearby, a sharp crash in the house, or a clatter that came without warning could send his attention snapping outward in alarm. He often reacted as if something terrible were about to happen even when nothing was actually wrong, and he recognized that the reaction came before his thinking caught up. His body would brace first — his heart racing, muscles tightening, his whole system shifting into readiness — and only afterward would he realize that he was safe. At times, the reaction became so vivid that he felt as if he were suddenly acting as though the disaster were happening again, as if the present scene had been overwritten by the old one.

Darnell’s response to these experiences gradually shaped the way he lived. He began avoiding anything that might be stressful, reasoning that if he could keep his days quiet and controlled, he might be able to keep himself steady. He turned down extra obligations, declined social gatherings when he anticipated noise or conflict, and tried to arrange his life so there were fewer surprises. Even at work, where he remained respected for his competence, he became more deliberate about limiting unnecessary demands and keeping his mind occupied from one task to the next. He told himself that constant mental busyness was safer than allowing his thoughts to drift, because empty moments gave room for the fragments of memory and the sudden sense of threat to intrude. At home, his wife noticed that he seemed always to be doing something — checking, organizing, watching television without really following it — as if he were trying not to be caught unprepared by his own mind. He also found himself eating excessively to manage distress, especially after a day that had left him keyed up or after a sound or exchange had unsettled him. The pattern brought him temporary relief, though he did not feel proud of it.

Over time, these habits narrowed his world. He became more cautious in ordinary places and more guarded in conversations where voices might rise. He still functioned, but with a growing sense that he had to stay on duty even when off the job. He was aware that his wife had begun to ask whether he was really present with her, and he did not like that his efforts to stay protected made him seem distant. What finally brought Darnell to seek help was a recent episode in which a sudden loud noise and shouting nearby made him react so sharply that he felt, for a moment, as if he were back in the disaster scene, body already in motion before he had time to think. He left unsettled and angry with himself, not only by how intense the reaction felt but by how familiar it had become. He came to treatment hoping to understand why his mind still held only broken pieces of the event and why his body kept warning him of danger when nothing was there, and he was most afraid that these moments would keep taking over his life and his marriage unless he found some way to make sense of them.
